utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. This is Thursday, October 23rd, 2008. I welcome Mr. Mundis, Ms. Biersay, Ms. Dahl also. On his right, I also welcome their case manager. And I greet Mr. Seselj. We are here to continue with the cross-examination of our witness, Mrs. Tabeau, but in the meanwhile I believe that the Office of the Prosecution has a housekeeping matter to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, to my learned colleagues, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Very briefly, there's a matter I feel needs to the drawn to the Trial Chamber's attention. Yesterday, before the commencement of the trial, the accused provided the Prosecution with a copy of his most recent book, "The Hague's Plucked Turkey: Christine Dahl." Because of its offensive nature, I'm not going to ask the AV booth to show this publication, but I do want to hand it up to the Trial Chamber and I ask you to please take a look at the cover of this book as well as briefly scan the contents. Your Honours, it's our submission and our position that the accused with the publication of this book has once again crossed the line. This book, especially its title and its cover, are offensive and it's our view that this conduct is a deliberate affront to the dignity of these proceedings, and it must stop now. In accordance with his oft stated -- oft repeated statements, the accused's mocking the international Tribunal. He is mocking this Trial Chamber. He is mocking the Office of the Prosecutor, he is mocking the victims, and mocking the international community as a whole. Outrages such as this must stop, and the Trial Chamber must take steps to bring this type of behaviour to an end once and for all. I would now ask if we could please go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, making this book a problem is quite simply not commensurate with these proceedings and bringing it up within these proceedings in trial. If Mrs. Christina Dahl considers that she is been labelled and that any evil has been done to her, she can have me up for slander with the court in Belgrade. She can file a criminal report, although in Serbia for verbal abuse there are no prison sentences that can be passed; it's just a monetary fine. And she can take me to court to seek compensation. The political methods during this trial, that is to say, to attack this book during the trial has absolutely no sense as well. The book was printed in 10.000 copies at the beginning of September, and you cannot ban the book through the courts because it has been distributed and almost all the copies have been sold out. You can't send someone from door to door to seize the books, nor do you know the list of purchases. And a large number of copies were handed out free of charge as the Serbian Radical Party does. Usually it hands out books free of charge or otherwise sells them at a symbolic price. So as far as the book is concerned, this Tribunal does not have the authority to deal with the matter, nor is it in order to raise that matter within these proceedings. I handed over a copy of the book yesterday to the Prosecution through the registrar because I wish to use the book while examining certain future witnesses. Whether they are going to appear as Prosecution witnesses or Defence witnesses is a matter I'll have to decide in due course. But I handed it over to the OTP yesterday. I could have handed it over in September, but I was in no hurry to do so. So I did that yesterday and I received just one copy, and a second copy arrived subsequently so that I was able to hand that one over later on. Now, as far as the title page goes or the cover of the book, that's up to the artistic vision of the person designing the cover. Someone might find it abusive; somebody else might look upon it with sympathy. If somebody did something like that to me, perhaps I'd be angry. Perhaps I'd just laugh it off. Perhaps I'd find it funny. Now, Mrs. Christina Dahl's attitude towards the cover page is up to her. If she considers that she has been done and can claim damages, then it's up to her to bring a lawsuit against me, but it comes under the authority of the court in Belgrade and that's it. That is the very end of it. Look at the list of books I've published to date, Mr. President. Just have a look at what I said about certain judges of this Tribunal in those titles. Have the Hrtkovci affair book provided to you by the Prosecution. It's a big book, so I can't carry it around. It's heavy. But you have a list of all my books there. See what I said about Judge Alphonsus Orie. I said much worse things than I did about Christine Dahl. I'm not going to read out the title, so you don't have to move into private session. What about the Registrar Hans Holthuis, what I said, and what I said about Carla Del Ponte. And what I said about that Justice Moloto, the Judge who asked in the Miletic trial, Why didn't you Serbs, when you weren't recognised by the Croats, didn't you go to Serbia where you are recognised? And several other examples. Judge Schomburg, for example, a whole title devoted to him, the title of the book, one whole book. So let them take me to court. Let them sue me. What I said refers to Christine Dahl is the mildest of my observations, and you can look at my collected works for that matter. Now, are you going to try me because of the titles of my book? All right, go ahead, try me for that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let's stop here. We have a witness and we have another witness listed for today. The Trial Chamber has heard you, has heard Mr. Mundis. Let me return this book to Mr. Mundis, because this was handed to the Prosecutor in the first place. What did you want to add, Mr. Seselj? THE ACCUSED [Interpretation] Since you've brought up administrative matters, two questions very briefly, ones that I'd like to raise. Yesterday I submitted to you a (redacted) (redacted), that I received the day before yesterday. I received it properly through the prison administration, and I handed it over to the registry so that it can be copied out for you. I hope that you have received a copy. No, it's not that paper. No, this is the one that I handed in this morning. Yesterday I handed over the letter so that it could be photocopied for the Judges and for the OTP. Today I brought in an order from the prison warden. You have it in the English language, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in private session

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, since you were surprised yesterday by the fact that I have been denied telephones for telephone communication with my legal advisors, I brought in this letter by way of proof. This is a letter from the prison warden sent to me on the 29th of September, 2008. On that day, on that evening, I had a scheduled conversation with my legal advisors at 1800 hours, or at 1900 hours. It doesn't really matter. I very properly asked the guard to have the line established and I sat there and waited for 10 or 15 minutes and then the guard came with the Registrar's letter and said that this became forbidden, conversations from that telephone. The same evening I received this letter from the prison warden. This is proof that I could no longer speak from that particular telephone. Before the 29th of September, on this list of telephone numbers, in addition to Bojan Gajic, who is the consul of the Republic of Serbia in Holland and who was in charge of us, The Hague convicts, he takes care of some administrative matters for us or whatever else, there was just the name of Slavko Jerkovic, too, on this list; that is to say, I could not contact all my legal advisors in the case, only Slavko Jerkovic. That is why I would have to schedule a meeting with Slavko Jerkovic and to say that the other members of the team should be in attendance as well and then we could all talk together. Well, from the 29th of September onwards, you see the date here, I have not been permitted to call Slavko Jerkovic from that telephone either. Now I can only call Bojan Gajic, the Serbian consul in the Netherlands, and no one else. That is what I told you about yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. The document is very straightforward and the Trial Chamber will review it. Let's have Ms. Tabeau brought into the courtroom. Let me remind you, Mr. Seselj, that you've already used one hour and 45 minutes. You have, therefore, 15 minutes left, but after consulting my fellow judges, we decided to grant you 15 additional minutes. In other words, you have half an hour left. I suppose there will be objections, questions by the Bench, and I suppose we'll need to go until 10, until the break. After the break there may be some re-examination, I'm not sure. But let's have Ms. Tabeau brought in. You have 30 minutes to complete your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I needed more time, but if that is your ruling, what can I do about it? I did need at least an hour more than the time that has been granted to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Tabeau. Please accept our apologies. You had to wait outside the courtroom, but we had a number of housekeeping matters to deal with. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to continue the discussion about your sources, Mrs. Tabeau. You used three basic sources - the book by Marko Kljajic, "The Parish Priest from Petrovaradin," based on information data from the records of the Hrtkovci parish office and information that you got from the Croatian authorities. Now, you did the matching of that, and it was fairly unsuccessful from the aspects of what you were looking at doing, matching of those three lists; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, the matching rates were not very high.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Mrs. Tabeau, why did you state here that the list of Marko Kljajic relates to the period 1992 to 1993 when Marko Kljajic had in mind a much longer period until the book was actually published and he incorporates people who had moved out after 1995? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list of 280 families you are referring to includes individuals who left Hrtkovci in 1992, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But just individuals; right? Now, when you had that book in your hands and saw on the second cover that Marko Kljajic was a Roman Catholic priest from Petrovaradin and that he had dedicated the book to the well-known notorious criminal and war criminal Franjo Tudjman, did a red light go on in your head? Did you have any suspicions to the effect that that book did not correspond to some moral or professional criteria and the aspiration to reach the truth and so on? Didn't it enter your head it might be propaganda with a political goal in mind?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use the book in my study. I used a list that was published in the book. And I knew that the source for the list is VS-61 and as such it was the same source as for parish records. And knowing that the parish records were not fully complete, not all requests were registered in the book. Naturally, this list was an expansion of the parish records that I also used in my study.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. But you attach here a letter by Bishop Ciril Kos addressed to the Serb patriarch. Didn't you wonder straight away and ask yourself, well, that it was obvious that they had a lengthy correspondence and then ask to see their previous letters, the patriarch's letters to Bishop Kos and other Croatian bishops, so that you could see what all this was about? Didn't you have any doubts and suspicions that it's quite obvious here that there had been previous correspondence and that the Serb patriarch appealed to the Roman Catholic Croatian bishops to become involved and prevent the persecution of Serbs by Tudjman's regime, and then at a point in time, Bishop Kos thought that he had an argument to answer with the same measure and to tell the Serb patriarch, It's not only that the Serbs are being persecuted over there, the Croats are being persecuted over here. Didn't that idea come to mind?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't study the correspondence between these two churches. What I was interested in was the statistical information that I needed for quantification of the departures from Hrtkovci. And at some point I decided that parish records is the right source and the best source I could use at that time for my study. And my purpose was to assess this source and the related list of 280 families. This is why I found the letter that was presented yesterday, together with the list, important and relevant. It is just yet another confirmation that the list was making sense, was real, and could be taken as a source for studying in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that every parish office of the Roman Catholic church has a logbook, a protocol book, in which entries are made of the reception of all documents and in which any documents being issued are recorded, entries of that are made?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what kind of logs the churches have. I believe it would make sense to have a log of incoming and outgoing correspondence. If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you should have consulted those logbooks because they can be proof in evidence that, for instance, in May a certain number of christening certificates were issued or marriage certificates or whatever. That would be a very good way of proving this. And do you know that in the records, the source records, no entries are made of when copies are made from those records, that is, recorded in the logbook, not in the records, parish records themselves? And I think the situation is the same in Poland or Holland. When you are given a copy issued from the -- of a marriage certificate or birth certificate, the very fact that this copy has been issued and extracted, it's not recorded in the basic records but in the logbook. Am I right in saying that, Mrs. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the very important fact is that church book itself, it is the primary document that really matters. And it is important because in this document information about individuals is complete, for instance, when it comes to baptism, a child is first born. There is a date of birth, place or date of the child, information about the parents, information about the christening, information about the godparents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This has absolutely no sense at all because we know that. You're just wasting my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This is not for Mr. Seselj to comment on, the quality of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We know everything that is entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If he could stop interrupting and allow her to finish, we could probably get through this more quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's for the Chamber to eventually rule on the quality of a testimony of this witness. Mr. Seselj, please put questions to the witness and let her answer. When it comes to the proper value of the testimony of this witness, it will be for the Judges to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you see, Mr. President, what I'm saying is this: Nowhere in the records are the entries made that extracts have been issued. In certain countries, for example, extracts have a three-month deadline and then you have to have a new extract issued. So the basic records do not contain entries of the extracts. This is done in a logbook. And the witness's answer to me is that she describes all the entries made in the basic record, in the register, in fact. So I'm saying that they were -- that the Prosecution has been, I fear, instructed to waste as much time as possible in my cross-examination because I won't have time to ask all my questions if the witness irrationally uses up all my time and says things that have nothing to do with my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, Mr. Seselj seems to be suggesting that you did not quite answer his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I want to finish what I started. So in these basic records there is information, the date of request, and in this way for me, for my statistical information, purposes, this is what I exactly need, all the information there. In addition to this, I have the list of the 280 families, and this can be seen as some kind of overview. It is an overview of the families who most likely all requested the certificates. I know that the request in the books are incomplete and this is why it makes sense to use the two things together. I don't need any separate log of incoming and outgoing correspondence made by this church.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Instead of drawing up the graph that is really rather frightening, you could compile the graph even if you had only five extracts being issued during the month of May. But anyway, didn't you ask yourself, since statistics is the science of large numbers, that you were now in a situation where your figures, your numbers, were too small? Seventy extracts issued in May, 17 in June; these figures are too small for you a priori to think that they are telling. The Petrovaradin Catholic priest Marko Kljajic and the priest from Hrtkovci could have sat down one afternoon and entered into the notes of the register all the data that you have taken as being true and correct. Nobody would accept them just like that, accept their validity without testing them and checking them out; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somebody instructed you, Mr. Seselj, to speak about statistics and big numbers in statistics, how important they are. But you are mixing up things. This report presents empirically observed data. It has nothing to do with estimating unknown parameters or unknown numbers. The issue of the sample size, how big it is, does matter in the statistical estimation of unknown information about the population in this particular case. I do work with real observed data, and the numbers produced in this report are minimum numbers. So is Annex A, the list in Annex A, and so are the distributions, the timing that I present. So your point is simply invalid in this case. And it is not true that any observed events must be big in order to make sense. If you think a little bit of situations in epidemiology for instance, there are diseases that the prevalence of which is really very, very low, so don't speak about sample size.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, I'm a layperson where demography is concerned, but don't tell me that I need instructions about the substance of the statistical method. I'm a doctor of science. I study the methodology of social sciences and I know what is meant by the statistical method. And the statistics of science is a science of large numbers only when -- and only when it compares certain groups with large numbers can the result be reliable. As soon as it boils down to small numbers, it is highly unreliable. But since you've gobbled up so much of my time and you did not heed my request, let's go to your expert report and Annex A. And may we have it placed on our screens so that we can go through your list there and see just how serious your work has been. You compiled the list by matching up two lists of the state authorities of Croatia from a list compiled by Marko Kljajic, allegedly on the basis of information and data of the register in Hrtkovci. And I'm just going to point to a number of examples which speak of imprecise unconsciousness and irresponsible work, and that is my initial thesis. Now I'm going to ask you concrete questions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the list brought up. It is Annex A. I now have the title page of the expert report, but I need Annex A. I have it here if the court administration doesn't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I believe it's at around approximately page 37 of the report, to assist the registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's the annex to the report, and additional section. And the title "List of Persons that Left Hrtkovci in Relation to the Events in May-August 1992," that's the title. Can we zoom into that please, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the first person on that list and let me repeat the title. "List of Persons that Left Hrtkovci in Relation to the Events in May-August 1992." Akrap, Anto, is number 1. He exchanged his property before those events and had a contract on the exchange which was recorded in Zagreb on the 10th of January, 1992. And you have that piece of information in the Croatian authorities records; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at number 5, Akrap Marija. Just like Akrap, Anto, the situation is the same, the 10th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Tabeau, let's go back to number 1. Mr. Seselj is submitting that this Anto Akrap would have exchanged his flat. This flat would have been swapped in January 1992. If he makes a swap, he leaves, so why is it that he is noted down as having left on December 15th, 1992? Of course assuming that what Mr. Seselj is saying is true, assuming, number 1, that there has been a contract to exchange flats, and 2, that Mr. Anto Akrap did say that he left in January 1992, because here we see December 15, 1992, the figures don't match.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said I don't have the information Mr. Seselj has, so this is what was my answer. It is -- I report what is reported in the refugee tables from the Croat authorities. And I don't have the contract related to the exchange of houses, so I simply don't know. In my statistics, he is reported in December 1992 as having left Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Look at number 3, Ivan Akrap. He reported that he no longer resided in Hrtkovci on the 19th of January, 1982, and he moved to Zagreb and then he registered residency on Zagreb on the 2nd of February, 1982. You have this information in the secretariat of the interior of Serbia and you also have the list of the Croatia authorities that were submitted to you. Did you have that particular information? Number 3 on your list.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are speaking of Akrap, Ivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ivan.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is reported in the list of family members that I received as additional to the list of 280 families, and in his record his first registration in Croatia is even earlier in 1982. I have no information in this record about his property. I don't know whether he exchanged property or not. I know that he most likely, according to the record, worked temporarily in Croatia and had an address in Croatia already before 1992. If he had a permanent address in Hrtkovci, he is reported in this record as having the permanent address in Hrtkovci. So this only means that he made a final decision in 1992 to leave the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why did you check with the Serbian authorities to see that he cancelled his registration in 1982? He is the son of Anto Akrap registered under number 1. He was born in Hrtkovci in 1982. He moved to Zagreb and he lived there. And then the 10th of January, in 1992, he was joined by his father, having signed a contract for the exchange of property. So your very own information shows what kind of forgeries you resort to. His son lived without interruption in Zagreb from 1982 onwards, and now in view of the fact that the priest Marko Kljajic only has a list of heads of households, since you know that he is a Kinsmen of this person, you artificially include him in this list of yours so that you would have a bigger list. Now, let's move on. Number 2, Gordana Akrap --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Tabeau, the list that we have here is a list that was drawn up by Croatian authorities. Number 3 is Mr. Ivan Akrap, who is the son of Ante Ivan, so everyone should think -- one can think and infer that the whole family is leaving at the same time - mother, father, son, and so on. But there's a problem with what we have on Ivan Akrap, and I did deal with this yesterday, I addressed the problem yesterday. We know that, in fact, he was registered in 1982 in Zagreb. I said that yesterday. And apparently he is living in Zagreb, and it's his father that is coming to join him. So putting him on the list as a person that could potentially be an expelled Croat can cast some doubt on this document. Didn't you think, you know, at the time that maybe in a household -- within a household some people in the household might already have left Hrtkovci, and that in this case what should have been done is to check on the City Hall registers whether his place of residence was actually Hrtkovci, to be a hundred percent sure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question on this. Yesterday we saw a document where we saw that there was -- he had a residence in Hrtkovci until 1992. Where did you get this information? There's an address, too, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Tabeau, when you take a look at this list made by the authorities, you see that the address in Hrtkovci is unknown. If this person is a refugee, he should give his previous address, and here it says "unknown," whereas we have the address in Zagreb. So this should have been checked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is -- first of all, Akrap, Ivan is reported with three family members as number 1 on the list of 280 expelled individuals from the book of Marko Kljajic. There is an address there. It is Lenova [phoen] Street, which is mentioned on the list, so obviously there is an address in Hrtkovci for this family. And on the other list that was received from a totally different source, from the Croatian authorities, there is no address in Hrtkovci. Obviously, the Croatian authorities didn't have the information about the address because probably the information was not given to them. I don't know what is the source for this. Well, it's further stated in the records from the Croatian authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but with this type of computation, when you add all the members of this 280 households, you end up with 722 individuals. But if Ivan Akrap was already residing in Zagreb, he should not be included in these 722. He is not a refugee. He was not expelled because of being frightened and so forth and so on. There may be others that are in exactly the same situation. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, two-thirds of the names on this list are that way. Two-thirds. And I have many other examples.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I want to comment here, first of all, the list of 280 families represents 805 individuals. For every family, the size of the family in Hrtkovci is reported. There is an address reported in Hrtkovci. So this list was not made up I believe because there are concrete pieces of information in there. I don't say that everybody in 1992 was living in Hrtkovci. I said yesterday and I'm saying today, it was quite a common situation in the former Yugoslavia that people who had permanent address of residence in one place were working and living in another place. And it was often done between people like here, living with permanent address in Hrtkovci but actually residing in Croatia. So that is how it was. But what does this mean? If the rest of the family -- son was in Zagreb, father and rest of the family or if not the entire rest of the family, then some family members lived in Hrtkovci, well, how should we consider cases of this kind? Whether it was a person who can be considered an expat or refugee or what, I believe these are people who eventually decided to leave the village, decided to exchange or were pushed into exchanging property --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, people. We do not contest the fact that people left the village. Number 24, for example, in the Colonel Gruzic's list, he has an address in Hrtkovci, so that's fine. For a number of them there are addresses in Hrtkovci. But we need to see exactly when they left Hrtkovci, whether they left Hrtkovci before or after May 1992. That's one problem. Secondly, the Croatian authorities do their job very well, like any other administration of course. But when I check this document, and Mr. Seselj is saying that there's two-thirds of them, I see that for a great number of people there is no address for Hrtkovci whereas there is an address for Zagreb, which leads me to wonder whether these people weren't already residing there in Zagreb. Why would Croatian authorities have the specific address for some and not for others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The address is available for everyone, every family. The address for Hrtkovci is reported on the list of 280 families. The list of family members is just an expansion of the list of 280. There is the link between these two lists. There is the family head, so the address is reported on the first list for family heads, also valid for all family members. It really doesn't matter that on the expansion of the list of 280 there is no address in Hrtkovci, because as a matter of fact, the address is available from the other list, from the list of 280. These are families, family members I was checking when comparing the list of family size. So the family size is different when you compare the size reported in the first list with the size reported in terms of family members. But the issue is complicated here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, proceed. We've heard your explanation. Thank you. We are in a rush, so please continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In relation to what the expert said, I just wanted to say that I'm just talking about residence, and that is a permanent category, whereas addresses are a temporary matter, and I'm not talking about that. Gordana Akrap, under number 2, she is a permanent resident of Croatia and has been so since 1973. You have that in the list provided by the Croatian authorities, right? Then number 4, Kata Akrap, she deregistered in Hrtkovci in 1980. You could have checked that at the municipality of Roma, and you didn't even try to do that. Number 6, Petar Akrap, he was born in Zagreb on the 29th of June, 1983. At that time on the 17th of July, two weeks after his birthday in 1938, he was registered as a resident of Croatia. He never changed his residency. You have it in your list provided by the Croatian authorities. Then Ankica Akrapovic, number 7, she never resided in Serbia, rather in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and she registered on the 4th of November, 1988, in Croatia. She has been living in Umag, Croatia, since then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I respectfully request that Mr. Seselj give the witness an opportunity to respond to what is now just merely assertions instead of compiling them in such a manner -- if he could do them singularly, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So he mentioned a number of cases. Could you please answer now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously Mr. Seselj has additional information about these individuals that I don't have. From my analysis of this data and familial relationship between the individuals reported on the first list and the individuals reported as family members, it was justified to include both the family heads and the family members in my list attached in Annex A. If there is additional information that I don't have that Mr. Seselj has, then I would really like to see it, because if it is the truth, what he is saying, then obviously a number of individuals have to be taken out of the list. But having this discussion without having this information doesn't make much sense because I must answer that I don't have this information, and in order to make informed decision, I need to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have mentioned some cases and very serious cases actually. You seem to say there are people that are on this list who had been who were no longer in Bosnia or Serbia for decades and who had been living in Zagreb and suddenly they appear on a list of expelled people. That's extremely serious because this could mean that these documents are forged. So where did you obtain this information, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, 04225 is the document that you should see, that's the 65 ter number. It was provided by the OTP. That's where the information is contained. Look at number 16, for instance. Let me just help you. Number 16 from the annex to the expert report, Nada Akrapovic. Please, on page 2 of this document, according to 65 ter, you'll find the name of Nada Akrapovic somewhere around mid-page. It says in that document that she was born in 1948 and that she lived in Belgrade - the address was Uzice number 4 - and that she moved to Croatia on the 22nd of February, 1994. Since then she has been a permanent resident of Zagreb. This is the list of the expert authorities, of the Croat authorities, that was provided to me by the Prosecution expert, you see that, and the OTP. You see that the expert cannot find her way in her own documents. She lived in Belgrade. In 1994 she moved from Belgrade to Zagreb. Two-thirds of them are that way. May I proceed now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on this specific case, this person living in Belgrade and arriving in Zagreb in 1994, what can you say on this person? Mr. Seselj, can you tell us exactly the exact page where we have this person? This person living in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Prosecution designation 04239016. I may have misspoken. 96, this is one of the lists provided by the Croatian authorities, the ones that I objected to yesterday and then you said that they should be marked for identification. So that is the list providing more detailed information. Have I been of assistance to you now? At least a bit. You have three lists from the Croatian authorities. The first one is the table with the very fine print, the second one is yet another table, and this is a list with more detailed information. And now on page 2 of that list, around mid-page, it says Nada Akrapovic lived in Belgrade; in 1994, moved to Zagreb. I don't have any information apart from the information that the expert witness has; however, I use the same information from her successfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, on page 2, Nada Akrapovic, there's an address in Belgrade. She was registered in Zagreb on February 2nd, 1994. That's what is written and reported. How is it that this happened -- how can we think that this person comes from Hrtkovci? What is the link?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The link is through the Ivan Akrapovic who is reported as number 3 on the first list, 280 heads. There are two Akrapovics - Akrapovic, Ivan, with six family members and Akrapovic, Ivan, with two - and they are both listed in the second list with the family members with Akrapovic Ivan, number 3, he is born on 11th of June 1974. Address in Serbia is unknown to the Croatian authorities, and he arrived in Croatia in August 1992 and has an address in Zagreb. And the other two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you did. You took the family head Ivan Akrapovic who lived in Ruma and left for Zagreb in August, and then you attached to this family head all those who were in the list of the Croatian authorities and who have the same name, the same surname. But that's extremely dangerous and perilous or risky. Because Nada, for example, Nada Akrapovic might be a member of this family, might have nothing to do with all this. She might not be involved by all the events. She might just decide to out of the blue to go to Zagreb in 1994, so why make a link here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who made the link? That is the answer. The link was made by the Croatian authorities who checked in the population register how many family members were associated with the family heads. For me, I'm taking the first list, 280 individuals who are culled and expelled persons from Hrtkovci and whom I know they were expelled in 1992 when they left Hrtkovci, departed from Hrtkovci in 1992. And I associate additional information about them and family members as obtained from the population registered in Croatia. And I want to explain a few things about the population register. It is the dates of registration in the register that should not be taken as the actual dates of arrival in Croatia. So this is why in our list in Annex A, we actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you here. Document 4225 is called "Information on Families Expelled from Hrtkovci." So anyone reading this would first read the title, see all these names, and at first sight would say this represents a great amount of people expelled from Hrtkovci. That is what you could infer at first sight. And then we'll find all that in the bar charts and in the statistical tables. But when you take a closer look at this, it doesn't always match. This Nada Akrapovic does not live in Hrtkovci, so you can't say she was expelled from Hrtkovci. She didn't live there. Can't you agree with me, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really because it is a matter of how you read the record of Croatian authorities. That she had an address in Belgrade at some point, first of all, we don't know when was it. I have no idea. What kind of timing here is involved, that is one thing. And as far as I can see, she registered in Croatia in 1994. Again, it doesn't tell me exactly when she departed. The only information about departure I have is from the family member, from the family head, which comes from the first list. So it's not that the information from the population register can be taken as resembling the actual population movement. And this I'm saying, people in the former Yugoslavia were not often working and living at the same place. The list that we are talking about, the family members was submitted to us as an expansion of the first list, 280 individuals of whom we know they were from Hrtkovci, of whom we know we have their addresses, and we know that they left Hrtkovci in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me look at another. Take a look at Ankica Akrapovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Belgrade. It can be seen that at the time she registered in Croatia she had an address in Belgrade. This could only mean that she could have moved between 1992 and 1994 from Hrtkovci to Belgrade and from Belgrade to Zagreb. That is not at all uncommon in the time of the conflict at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me take another example. Ankica Akrapovic. Address is Kacuni, it's Kacuni. Kacuni is not Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And she is recorded on November 4, 1988. I get the impression that when a family, when a head of family left Hrtkovci, of the relatives attached to that family who may be in Croatia, end up in Croatia. And then we have a list and the conclusion is that they were all expelled from Hrtkovci. But when you detail it all, when you look into details and look at all the different families, it's a bit different. It seems to be more complicated than that. You know, when you do your work properly as a judge -- do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a different opinion on this. For instance, if you look at this Akrapovic, Ankica, and you look at the family head, it is Akrapovic, Stipo, one record earlier on the list. And the address of Stipo is also in Bosnia and Herzegovina. His arrival in Croatia is 1993, as you see, and it is, in my eyes, perfectly possible that he left Hrtkovci in 1992 as reported on the first list, moved to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and eventually from Bosnia he moved to Croatia. And because he was in Bosnia, he cannot be reported as a refugee because it is already his second country of destination. And in this case absolutely impossible to include such a person as a refugee. So what I'm trying to say, reconstructing the migration history is a very difficult task. This is why initially the plan for this project was to compare the census data and to study the records of people known not reported at the later census in the registers of displacement. And this is a source that is most certainly relevant, but it shouldn't be taken literally as the reported dates have a more complex context than what we think should be in there. This is all I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand what you are saying because in your theory, these people might have an address some place and go through Hrtkovci at one point in time, which is why I asked you yesterday whether you went to take a look at the registers in town hall, whether you went to take a look at the tax records, tax registers to get, you know, a formal proof of all this. But you told me that you did not check all these registers. But we cannot draw conclusions if we don't have -- if we are not a hundred percent sure. And I can only be a hundred percent sure if I have an address in Hrtkovci on this document. It's straightforward. But if there's no address in Hrtkovci, this is going to cast doubt in my mind, of course. I'm going to wonder whether things really happened like I'm told, like you are telling me, especially -- the title of the list is "Expelled People." If these people were truly expelled, I need at least to know a hundred percent sure that the person was residing there in 1992. I'm sure you understand me. I'm not going continue on this because it's 10.00. Unfortunately, Mr. Seselj, you have one minute left. Well, you have 15 minutes. We had 15 additional minutes, so you will have 15 additional minutes after the break, but please be fast. Maybe Mrs. Biersay will have additional questions. Mrs. Biersay, do you think you'll have additional questions, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For how long?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think I can do it in less than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have another witness scheduled.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since I'm not going to waste any of our time with that second witness and as Biersay has said she'll just take 15 minutes, may I be given a little more time now? Because I really have some very important questions to ask, and I don't think any of the question that I've asked so far were insignificant. You can't say that about any of my questions. And we are dealing with an expert witness. So I did make an effort to save time with many witnesses beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll try to do some math. Our goal is to hear witness -- the second witness under Rule 92 ter, so just a few questions are put to this witness. We will also want Mrs. Biersay to put some additional questions because she needs time for that. We'll do some math over the break. We will see if we can give you 30 minutes instead of 15 minutes. We'll check on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session without Judge Lattanzi, who has to attend to some other business. But we'll proceed with the hearing according to the rules with the two other judges of the Bench. Mr. Seselj, please proceed. According to my math, you have until 11.00, provided there aren't any objections. The Judges will refrain from asking questions in order for us to hear this witness and the following witness. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, take a look at the number 18, and you'll find the name Alisa Andrasek. She didn't move out of Vojvodina at all. She moved from Hrtkovci and set up residence in the neighbouring village of Platicevo. And here she is in the pre-electoral campaign of the Serbian Radical Party for the local elections in the Ruma municipality. She is involved there, whereas you have put her on the list of expelled persons. Why? That's number 18 I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the information you have. Perhaps if I had it, I would have changed my mind. But, Your Honour, if I may comment on the discussion we had just before the break. I wanted to close this discussion with some other remarks, very brief, if I may. I would like to direct your attention to Table 13 in my report, page 26.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are wasting my time again, Mr. President. This is on my time, time that I was at pains to regain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It won't be deducted from your time, Mr. Seselj. Please proceed quickly, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This list contains an overview of the records in Annex A, the 722 [indiscernible] accepted records for refugees; 116 address in Hrtkovci is all known and available. For family heads accepted, 266 addresses in Hrtkovci, known and available. For family members, 88 addresses uncertain. Not for all. It is a maximum that for 88 addresses in Hrtkovci wouldn't be available and known. For a number is unavailable, unknown. Christenings and marriages 170, 82; address in Hrtkovci, available from the church books. So the answer that you were talking about relates to up to the maximum of 88 records. The information from Croat authorities shouldn't be read as to point -- as pointing exactly to the dates of the departure and residence at the time times reported in this records. The information was provided to us as available to the Croat authorities. Addresses and dates were reported in the past and relate to different time periods and not to the time period we are talking about, that is, 1992. That is all I wanted to say, and I hope this is useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Science -- in science you just have to have reliable data. Science doesn't cater to speculation, and this kind of speculation is something that not even philosophy can take. Maybe theology, but not that either. Look at number 34. Baric, Ana moved to Austria before the war and is still living there. All the inhabitants of Hrtkovci know that. Have you ever been to Hrtkovci, Mrs. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've never been and never tried to see and investigate matters in the field? All right. Perhaps that comes within the scope of the framework of the methods you have applied. Now, the next name we have, 35, Ana Baric. She is a permanent resident of Croatia and has been from the 25th of May, 1970. You will find that in the list compiled by the Croatia authorities.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my comment is you shouldn't read this list literally, Mr. Seselj. It is -- what matters is the personal information about the individuals, and the rest is not necessarily relevant and exactly as it should be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You can't know in advance, Mrs. Tabeau, what is relevant and what isn't. You compiled and submitted your expert report and the annexes, and I am proving that that is unreliable, because if we were to take you at face value, that would support the indictment. However, since I'm refuting the indictment, I'm refuting your report, too. Now, let's look at number 48. That is Ljubisa Baric. In 1974, on the 1st of February, she moved from Hrtkovci to Preboj, and Preboj is a town in Serbia, along the Drina river. So had you checked this out in the Ruma municipality, you would have had that information. But since you didn't travel there, then this priest from Petrovaradin seems to be the main source of your information. Now look at Petar Baric. I assume that's her husband. He moved to Preboj on the 31st of January, 1974. Number 37 on your list. Now take a look at number 70, Katica Baricevic. She appears on your list twice. Also number 464, she's the same person but changed her surname to Paulic when she married. You could have established that in the marriages register in Hrtkovci. Now, look at number 77.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. Was there -- what was the question to Madam Tabeau with respect to the first one he mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have identified a number of cases. Please put your question to the witness now because otherwise we are going to get lost and lose the thread and Ms. Biersay will object. And then you can proceed with other examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, my question was implicitly contained in the observation. Why is Katica Baricevic on the list twice, having married and changed her surname? Just to increase the number of names and numbers; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is unjustified, what you are saying. First of all, I didn't have the opportunities to check the records. Then I could answer. But more generally, I would like to say it is not that I wanted to increase the size of the individuals listed. I explicitly say in my report the list might be first incomplete, but on the second hand, it can also contain duplicates because the information of such individuals is not complete, certain pieces of information were not there. I note even approximately 40 potential duplicates that are now included in the list. Of these 40, I know a number are not duplicates because even though they are listed with identical names, they have different addresses in Hrtkovci. So my marking of potential duplicates should be seen to you as being honest and not inflating the size of the list. I think I did it conservatively because I know that a number of these records are not duplicates, but I still mark them as potential duplicates in the list. So I think you should read my report very carefully and then you would see that it is not what I'm doing, what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I hope, Mrs. Tabeau, that it has become quite clear to you what I think about your honesty. So let's leave that subject to one side. I don't want to speak about that now. Now, look at number 77 and 78. You took one and the same person and that person's name is Gabor Bartok. And then with number 78 you put Gavra Bartok, as if it's a female, whereas it's the same person, the same man. His name is Gabor and his nickname is Gavra, given to him by the Serbian community where he lived. Gavra is a male name, a man's name, not a female name. Perhaps it is exists somewhere. But anyway, you list one person in two places, and in the first place you say it's a man, for sex, and in the second one, you say woman, whereas -- and the date of birth is the same, whereas no twins like that were born ever in Hrtkovci; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure at all that Gabro and Gavra is one and the same person. To me these names are different. And I have a native B/C/S speaker in my unit who was looking at the names and who decided whether or not the names can represent one and the same person or not. My answer is perhaps you know more about it than I do. But from the names I wouldn't decide these are exactly the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you didn't check it out on the ground, in the field, nor did you go to the official state registers to check that out. Now, take a look at number 82, Lucija Batista. Everybody in Hrtkovci knows that she's been living and working in Germany since before the war, so how come you put her on this list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yet again, it telling me things based on common knowledge or source that I don't have at my disposal. In order to be able to respond to what you are saying, I would need these additional information. That is all I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you should have checked it out so that you can stand by every name that you put on the list. You should have investigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, if we look at the case of Ms. Batista who, according to Mr. Seselj, is currently working in Germany, we may suppose that through his own investigators, he checked that very fact. That's what he found out after conducting an investigation. I don't have the relevant documents, but I would find it difficult to believe that he could state something completely false, because if it appears that this lady does not work in Germany, then it would mean that Mr. Seselj had lied. Of course I understand that you were not in a position to check this particular information. It may very well have been that the OTP should have conducted such checks, but it was not done. That's all we can say about this matter. But you did not exclude the possibility of duplicates or mistakes in these lists; you've stated that yourself and we take due notice of that. But if what is being said about Mrs. Batista is correct, then it appears that this lady could not have left Hrtkovci as an expellee. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, is it possible -- then how is it possible --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I just add one thing. Not anywhere on the list of the Croatian authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let the witness complete her answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is that this person has reported based on the parish books, christening records, and I'm asking myself why this person would request for the certificate on the 16th of May, 1992. Well, I did not investigate this case in Germany, I must admit I didn't, as I didn't investigate all other cases. That is an impossible task for a person like me. I have to rely on some resources, statistical resources, and this is how this report was made. But if Mr. Seselj has additional information which I will find reliable, I'm prepared to revise the list. It is the only answer. It is not that I think this report was made to help understand what happened in this village, and I still see this report as such. The only purpose of my work is to bring a better understanding. So whatever more information is available, I will most certainly take it into account and revise Annex A and whatever else is necessary. That's all I can say. As of now I haven't received anything that I can work with. That is where we are today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it never crossed your mind that two Catholic priests very nicely forged information within the campaign that was carried out. You simply take everything from them at face value; right? Look at 93, Martin Begic. In 1970 he moved from Hrtkovci to Sabac. Had you checked in the municipality of Ruma, you would have found proof of that; namely, his deregistration in the municipality of Ruma. Martin Begic. But you didn't check anything, did you? And since he is not on the list of the Croatian authorities, wouldn't that be an indicator to you to become suspicious of what the priests gave you? Am I not right? Just say yes or no and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not right. In my eyes, it was not my task to investigate every single person. If I would have to investigate, for instance, Srebrenica victims, I would be busy investigating the first 1.000 victims as of now and there would be a few more thousand to go. So that is not the way -- how things are done in these days, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take the example of Begic. According to Mr. Seselj, he left Hrtkovci in 1970. I'm not sure if this individual requested a christening or marriage certificate, but let's assume that Mr. Seselj and his investigators find Mr. Begic and ask him whether he filed an application for a christening certificate. Let's assume that Begic responds, I've never requested a baptism certificate or christening certificate. What would be the impact of this from a statistical perspective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it is, first of all, not realistic to believe that parish records are made up, so I think that the information from parish records is detailed and correct. And there is a note of Mr. Begic's request for certificate on the 28th of May, 1992, so this is what we see in the records. What would be the impact here? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, yes. Yes, we have a record here showing that he made that request on the 28th of May, 1992. But when you are a judge worth his salt, when you do your job properly as a judge, and that's what I hope to be doing, you need to check things and you need to check first if Mr. Begic, indeed, made that request on the 28th of May, 1992. If he made that request, fine. But if he did not requested such a certificate, then we have a question posed about this register, this parish book and this record and this entry in the register. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned Srebrenica. You appeared there as an expert witness, too, and you took part in falsifying the information concerning the number of executed prisoners in order to create a background for declaring genocide. This is how you did it: You included more than 1.000 persons on the list of executed persons who had actually lost their lives before 1995; then also you included many persons who lost their lives during the breakthrough from Srebrenica to Tuzla; then you also included the victims of the inter-Muslim fighting; and then you resorted to different statistical finesse, and one is proverbial, comparing the 1991 census from there and the 1997 election lists or lists of voters. You did all of that in order to artificially increase the number of victims in Srebrenica and to create a basis for declaring falsely the genocide had been carried out there. That's right, right? Okay. Now we move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, this objection is sustained. We are not dealing here with events that happened in Srebrenica, Tuzla, and so on and so forth, and not expected to rule on this. Our expert witness is here to testify solely on the study she conducted about Hrtkovci, and it's solely on that basis, on the basis of that report, that we should decide whether the work was conducted properly, whether it should be completed or not. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Number 96, you have Tomislav Begic, and on the 10th of October, 1991, he was in Zagreb and he registered his contract to exchange immovable property. Why didn't you check that in Zagreb? You just have his first registration here, the one that took place almost a year later in 1992. However, he registered his contract on the exchange of immovable property already in 1991. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you give me this contract, exchange contract, then I can tell you more about this case. Again, it's your reading and your interpretation of the data provided to us by the Croatian authorities, and I have a different interpretation and different perspective on this data. So I think before you can draw any conclusions at all, you have to submit the additional information that you have that would support the conclusions you are drawing from this data. As of now, I absolutely don't accept what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, you would have had that contract on your screen had I not been dis-communicated from my associates. 110, Blazic, Ana Blazic, she never moved from Hrtkovci. She died there in 1999. And you could have established that in the death register in the municipality of Ruma, not with those preachers of yours in Ruma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let's return to this contract, assuming that there is such a contract, and if you mention it, I suppose that you checked that. This contract was drawn up in 1991, so that person may have left for Zagreb in 1991. Therefore, it is not related to what happened in 1992. But Ms. Tabeau is right in saying that nothing proves that this person was still -- was not in the village. So you are right and she is right. What should have been done is check with Tomislav Begic exactly when he settled in Zagreb. This should have been checked by the OTP, by the Defence maybe, but as things stand, both of you are right. It's extremely difficult to decide which way to go. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I'm always in favour of believing the Prosecutor and the OTP because they are the truth-loving people in this Tribunal. Why did you include this person under number 110 in your list when she never moved out of Hrtkovci and she died in 1999? You don't even know that she died, right? Because you didn't carry out any kind of onsite investigation. You never consulted the official books there and registers, right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If she died, I would have seen a record of her death in the books and I would have taken this record for my database, so that would be if she was part of the Catholic church, registered simply in these books.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You did not consult the death register at all. The death register is kept by the municipality of Ruma, not by the church, and it is not the obligation of every Croat to be a Catholic or to be buried according to religious rights. That is yet another reason for the unreliability of your church records. There's only one proper source and that is the death register of the municipality of Ruma. We are not in a theocracy to proclaim church records as official records, and we have seen how preachers can falsify that in a single afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If Mr. Seselj could just restrict his comments to questions instead of lecturing the witness, we could be done with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Number 112, Antun Blazic. You put him on the list of allegedly expelled persons whereas he never moved out of Hrtkovci. He died in Hrtkovci in 1999, and that was registered in the death register in the municipality of Ruma. And you don't even have that piece of information, right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, you know that I didn't use the death register, and if I had a record in the parish books -- and I would have the record in the parish book if he died and was buried in the Catholic church, and I would most certainly exclude him from the list. But you said he died in 1991, right, in Hrtkovci, so he never left, so you are saying that --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said, 1999. But your point is that there are people who never left Hrtkovci and are on the list. Well, it is possible there are people who never left Hrtkovci on my list. There might be a few. But on the other hand, if you look at the census in comparison to the size of the Croat population, then you see that 250, 250 approximately are still there. Whether they are the same persons, I hope, yes. That not everybody left the village, but I don't know because I didn't study this, who was going, who was staying in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Don't turn things the other way around. I'm not challenging the fact that many Croats left Hrtkovci having exchanged their property, but your list about them is highly unreliable so these are two completely different matters. Your heading here should have been "The List of Persons who had Certificates of Birth or Marriage Issued to Them," not as you did. Vesna Blazic, 116. In the meantime she got married and now her last name is Vujicic. Obviously she is married to a Serb. She lives in the neighbouring village. She never left Vojvodina, and to this day, she works as a teacher in Hrtkovci. Vesna Blazic, number 116 on your own list, she is a teacher in Hrtkovci to this day. This is not quite reliable. I think that she is also a member of the Serb Radical Party, but I'll check that. Why did you put her on the list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because she is in the christening records, and she requested a certificate in 1992. This is why I put her on the list. Why would she do that, I don't know. Perhaps she, after all, changed her mind. Obviously in 1992 she requested a certificate. After all, she wasn't feeling that safe if she made this decision to be prepared for living. So this is how the parish records should be read. This is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have no proof whatsoever of her having asked for a certificate. The fact that some preacher later on recorded it, that is not proof that she actually asked for it, whereas you should have investigated on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if we look at 116, the case of Vesna Blazic, apparently your associates conducted a number of investigations about this person. It would appear that she is now a teacher in the same village. All right. She may even be a member of your own party. All right. But if that's the case, what prevented you and your team from going to see that lady to ask her whether indeed in 1992 she requested a christening certificate? Two things may have happened. She may have said, I requested a certificate for such and such a reason, or secondly, she may have said, I never made that request. Why didn't your investigators conduct -- do that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My investigators probably already took care of that. But for a month now I haven't had any communication with them. Even when they start telling me something in relation to this trial, I stop immediately. I say, No, no, don't talk about that. We are being eavesdropped on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ruzica Bogovic is someone who you placed on your list twice, 128 and 691, but under her maiden name Velez. You could have established that in those preacher books of yours, of marriages. So it is 128 and 691. Then 133, since this is a duplicate as well, I'll link it up. It says "Mirjana Damjanovic," who also appears under number 513 as Mirjana Radocaj. Why did you --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry. I'm unable to follow these records because Mr. Seselj is proceeding so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I'm standing up to ask the Court to require that Mr. Seselj pose a question to the witness instead of testifying, which is essentially what he is doing. We would also strongly object to any reliance on Mr. Seselj's assertions, factual assertions, about the status of these people absent any records provided to either the witness or to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I've already told you, in order to avoid objections by the Prosecution, you have to put questions to the witness. For example, Witness, I'm looking at the case of number X on the list and I find such and such thing, and so on and so forth. Please put actual questions to the witness and to avoid wasting time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I pointed out that I want to link up two cases because they are identical in terms of the nature of the forgery involved, because the same persons appear on this list twice but under different surnames because they got married in the meantime. The first one got this new last name, Velez, and then the other one got the last name of Radocaj. I've given the numbers already. Let me move on to the next question because this I've done in vain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Number 172, you have Zlatko Damjanovic. According to my information, he is abroad in Germany. He lived there from before the war and he registered his residency in Croatia on the 11th of November, 1999; that is to say, from Germany he went back to Croatia and registered there. You have him on the list of Croatian authorities. Why did you put him on the list of expelled persons from Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I didn't have your sources, Mr. Seselj. And as long as I don't have these sources, I can't say anything. I'm still having trust in the sources I use and in the records I place on my list, and I can only say when I will receive additional information I'm able to revise what I presented. That's all. I'm not taking your words for granted, sorry, but you have to give me something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, yes, I have this list that you gave to me, the list by the Croatian authorities. You can see Zlatko Damjanovic there, first registered in the Republic of Croatia on the 11th of November, 1999, in Bjelovar, Tomar Bakrav [phoen] Street, number 38. There you have the information. You could have checked that out in your own documentation had you been conscientious in fulfilling your task. Have you found him?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're wrong in saying I had information on Zlatko Damjanovic from the Croats. He reported on the basis of christening. Damjanovic, Zlata is a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Come on, please. Here he is on the list compiled by the Croatian authorities. Here he is on the Croatian list. The last two figures, 29, you can see that for yourselves, Judges. What we've already looked at, 29 are the last digits. And the number -- it's under number 54. And I should assume it should be 54 after that as a family member. In 1999 he was registered in Croatia. Furthermore, why on the list do you have 189 as being Antun Engert?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. For Zlatko Damjanovic, in the Croatian document, he has an address in Hrtkovci. Nazoro Street, number 26.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Mr. President. But in 1999 he moved to Croatia. In 1999 you have the information right below that. They have not got the information that he worked in Germany, so that's my additional information, that he worked in Germany from before the war. But in 1999 he came to reside in Croatia, and that's what it says there, too. I'm not challenging the place of birth, his place of the birth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Tabeau, above there's Zlata. This person must be a relative. I see that Zlata is born on March 6th, '24, whereas Zlato is born in 1950. So Zlato is probably Zlata's son. However, if Zlata lives in Hrtkovci, the Croatian authorities maybe put his residence in Hrtkovci, even though he is working in Germany. Could that be an explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course this can be an explanation, but we don't know what the Croat authorities really did when it comes to addresses and dates. He is included in my list based on christening records, not on the records of the Croatian authorities or the records from the refugee tables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a judge could infer, could have the following explanation: This Zlata leaves Hrtkovci on July 14, 1993. We don't know when he left, but he is registered on July 14, 1993. Now, maybe Zlata at that point in time asked the priest for all christening certificates of the entire family, of the entire household, and he was provided with these certificates. And his son Zlato, who according to Mr. Seselj works in Germany, would have left Germany in 1999 and would then be registered in Croatia in 1999. That would be one explanation of all this, which would mean also that Zlato had not been expelled from Hrtkovci. Maybe his father was but not him. Otherwise, the Croatian authorities would have recorded him on July 14th, 1993, both father and son.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is one of the complex cases for which we don't know the migration history and, well, according to the approach taken in my report, Zlata and Zlato are reported from two different sources. Zlato is a refugee. He's taken based on the christening. I don't want to speculate about the migration history. But, again, it is if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem with the other brother, Zdenko. He is recorded on September 24, 1996. I don't know where he lived, where he was, but there could also be a problem with him, with Zdenko. However, Rijana [phoen], who might be the daughter, was recorded on February 18. Then there's Adrijan, another relative, who is recorded on August 27, 1999. So it's quite complex.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I'm saying. It is a complex situation. If you look, Your Honours, on the address in Hrtkovci, it's all the same address. Obviously it is a family living in one and the same place in Hrtkovci. And it is possible that some members of the family --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. Let's assume the father lives in Hrtkovci but all the others might be scattered anywhere else. So who is expelled here? It's the father, not the other members since they are elsewhere. Unless you decide that when expelling one -- the father, you expel the entire family, even if some relatives live in Canada at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why, under 189, did you put the name of Antun Engert when he died in Hrtkovci in 1991? And his death was recorded in the register of deaths in Ruma municipality. E-n-g-e-r-t. Because those preachers gave you that piece of information. Perhaps that priest was under the influence that day when he provided you that data, and you're taking it as all being true and correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj asked: "Why, under 189, did you put the name of Antun ..." Could the witness please be allowed to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
