utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please answer. It seems that this person died in 1919, so why is it on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no record in the death -- parish book of the death, and he is reported in my list based on the request for marriage certificate that was made on the 7th of June, 1992. That is the answer. And I didn't check the death registration in the municipality of Ruma, and according to Mr. Seselj, if I had done this, I would have information about the deaths. I believe that deaths are also parallel-registered in the parish books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there's danger in focusing only on the church records. If this person died in 1991, maybe a relative, a son or daughter, for problems that have to deal with inheritance or other problems, might need a certificate, and then goes to the church to ask for this church record on June 7th, 1992, and you can draw the conclusion that he had asked for this certificate because he was being expelled. You could draw this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe my fellow Judge had a question to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, I had the same problem and the same question to you that the Presiding Judge just put to you, because it seems to me, in reviewing the parish list, that of course the parish list is not complete, and you have stated this at several locations in your report and during the testimony here. I think that is a fact that is easily accepted by the Chamber. The difficulty, however, comes from the title of the document, because the title seems to suggest that the people who are mentioned in the list actually left Hrtkovci, and that is a conclusion that may not be warranted necessarily by the fact that Croats in Hrtkovci required from the priest certain certificates, either of birth or marriage or whatever. That is the shortcoming that I see in the importance and significance of this list. Can you give us a brief comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is in the church records, the dates for requests, I said several times should be seen as proxies for certain decisions related to the departure. It is not that the decision to be ready to go is exactly the same as just going. And as I said earlier in my testimony, I didn't see -- or documents or myself -- buses taking these people away and soldiers escorting these people to the border, so it is not what I'm saying. I'm saying this is a good proxy for the decision, and it's possible that some of these people didn't even leave the village, but a majority of them did because this is what we see from other sources as well. And it is a matter of the timing of the departures. Ideally we would like to see a data of the dates when these people were going away and places where they went to, but that is not possible. I don't have this data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I accept that. I accept that fully. Of course we will give the weight to this list that we will determine in the end. The only problem is that the title of the document suggests that these people actually left and so that's why I feel that the title of the document is slightly misleading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think this is also Mr. Seselj's point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is an issue here. The issue related to the fact that physically these people who are reported on the list, not all were at Hrtkovci at the time of the events and I'm not saying they were all there, physically speaking. However, here is the question: If there is a family that is composed of six people, there is a mother, father and four children, and two of these children are studying, one in Belgrade and one in Zagreb, two others are working, one in Bosnia and one somewhere in Vojvodina, not necessarily in Hrtkovci; there comes 1992, the political situation becomes unstable and difficult, and the family, the parent physically being there, decides it's time to go because it is too risky to stay. Then a decision is made as a matter of fact for the entire family. The question not to me but I'm afraid to Your Honours and to this Chamber is how to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree with what you are saying. If the father and the mother decide to leave, they decide for themselves. It's their decision. If their children are minors, fine, I agree with you. But if their children are adults and live and work elsewhere, you cannot claim that because the father and the mother decided to leave, the entire family left. I cannot agree with this interpretation because I believe it goes too far. They can take a decision for a minor, that's fine, but they cannot make a decision for their relatives who are adults who might be living in other cities, who might be in other places, and who might not have made the same decision had they been in Hrtkovci. We don't know anything there. I believe that with your interpretation, you inferred that if the head of the household decided to leave, the entire family left. So I'm saying, Okay, for minors but not for adults, because I believe there is a problem. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I add one comment? There is the issue of the family, and there is intergenerational transfers. It is a very well-known fact that people who were working in western countries were transferring money, and a lot of it, to families back home, and houses and property was mainly coming from these extra sources. And the same with children. It is not that the children are able to finance themselves when studying. So the families, I think in the western family, it is indeed minors, end of story. But we are speaking of a family in a totally different environment. We are speaking of a family in a little village, Hrtkovci, in a country which is exceptional among all post-communist countries. You are speaking of a country when the borders were open since the beginning of the 1970s, and people were travelling freely were making money and bringing money a lot of properties were paid with this money. So the family is different. It's the traditional family. It is multigenerational families living in the one house. The house belongs to the entire family. This is my rationale behind this list. So I didn't want to mislead anybody. But we are speaking of a totally different family situation here compared to western countries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why, under number 263, did you put the name of Kata Ilic, when up to 2003 she lived in Opovo [phoen]? That is also in Vojvodina but in a region called Banat. And on the 27th of November, 2003, she moved to Croatia and you have her on this list of -- of the Croatian authorities list under number 90. So in 2003 she came to reside in Tejn [phoen] near Osijek, obviously exchanging her property because Tejn was a Serbian village near Osijek. So she's number 90 on the Croatian list, and on your list, she's number 263.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I have to explain this again in exactly the same way. In my list she's taken from the family heads. That is what I see here on the list. And there is additional information and she's reported in 2003 by the Croat authorities. Again, it is a misreading of the Croatian sources, as far as I can see. That is all I can say. We can proceed like this record by record, but I think that this will not change the basic principle I used to make this list, and it will not have any impact on what I said so far about these sources and about the records included based on these sources. And so once again, if there is more information, please give it to me. I will look into it and assess it and revise, if necessary. But on the other hand, I still stand behind the principle and the sources I used for this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm absolutely opposed to you changing your report subsequently. The Prosecution can engage a new expert. You had your opportunity. You had the chance to change your report before testifying. Why, under number 264, do you have the name of Milan Ilic when he didn't live in Hrtkovci but in Platicevo? And you have him under number 91 on the Croatian list, and there it says that his address was Platicevo, in Platicevo, whereas you list him as a Hrtkovci inhabitant. Number 264 is what I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is listed in my list based on the family head records. He is reported as departed to Croatia in 1992, and in the Croatian records the other list, it is number 92. He is reported in Platicevo, but I can't see here the date when he was -- he is reported from Platicevo, in Serbia, but there was no date when he was registered in Croatia. So I have no idea whatsoever when --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what do we care when he left Platicevo. The important thing is that he didn't leave from Hrtkovci. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is that in family heads he is reported in Hrtkovci with an address. So the point is that the address given in the Croatian records, we don't know to which time, moment, it refers. So it is perfectly possible that the person left Hrtkovci in 1992, moved somewhere else within Serbia, and after that moved a second time from Serbia to Croatia. Anything is possible as long as we can document it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have the time left, Mr. Registrar. I'm worried about the time. Mr. Seselj, I believe that your time has run out, so please speed up. Move to the core of your question. I mean we could review all these cases one by one. It would take forever. Please put a question that would sum up the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I think that these special cases are the most effective way of challenging the entire expert report. This is key evidence to the lack of seriousness on the part of the expert and her report. I have a few more significant examples. You know, yesterday when I made all these attempts to have an expert discussion with the expert, all of that proved futile because she gave answers that were way too extensive, and also I'd ask one thing and she'd say something completely different in reply. Now she has no way of dealing with it when she's put specific questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your question and quote the numbers of the relevant cases. Put your question and the expert will answer. You've used up 2 hours and 37 minutes so far. You've now almost had 40 minutes more than the Prosecution had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Under number 364, why did you put the name of Antun Ledenko when he exchanged his property on the 14th of November, 1991, and the contract on the exchange of immovable property was registered? Antun Ledenko.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is included based on the family head's record as departed to Croatia in 1992, and I didn't have the exchange contract, Mr. Seselj, which if you give it to me, I will look through it and assess it and possibly, or not, revise my list. It depends on what you would give me. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it more important for you to study the exchange of -- registers of contracts on exchanges than to focus on information that was fabricated by the two parish priests? You were only interested in that, nothing else. If other objective sources testified to the contrary, so much the worse for the objective sources. Jure Mrkonja, why did you put that name on your list when he exchanged his property and on the 5th of November this contract was registered in Zagreb? You could check that with the Croatian authorities. On the 5th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number is it on my list?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 411. 411 on your list, the list of those whom I expelled from Hrtkovci, as you say. List of my victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection. The witness made no such statement these people were expelled by Mr. Seselj. That is an allegation that we make in the indictment, but this witness has never said such a thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the record, number 411, Mrkonja, Jure. Based on the family heads table, he is included in my list as departed from Hrtkovci in 1992 and heading to Croatia. That was his destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, isn't it possible that he exchanged property in 1991, and in 1992, when he needed that for obtaining Croatian documents, he then asked for an extract from the birth register in Hrtkovci? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is not registered in my list based on the parish records. It is family heads list. Well, I think I'm feeling very uncomfortable with the questions related to the exchanges because the exchanges is something that goes beyond this report. I didn't study this and I don't have data on this, and moreover, I don't have the contextual information about how the contracts were made. So I think it is not a fair question to ask me to comment on this. It's just not my subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber is fully informed of all this. We've understood the problem. This lady did not know about the contracts. We know that she worked from three sources only, and we see, as we look at a few cases, that there are some problems. Everyone is fully aware of this now. You've used up 2 hours and 40 minutes. You may ask one last question, but I'm going to cut you off very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, madam. I hope you are in a position to hear what I'm saying in your own language. I would like you to stand up because I'm going to ask you to read the solemn declaration. Please give me your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Have you ever testified before a court about the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia, or is it the first time you've testified about these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before I give the floor to the Prosecutor who will apply the 92 ter procedure, I have a number of questions to put to you. I know that you are Serb. Before you came here to testify before this Tribunal, have you received any telephone calls? Have you met people who tried to intimidate you in order to convince you not to testify, or is it the case that no one got in touch with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no such calls, nor did anybody attempt to do any of those things or to prevail upon me not to testify or to influence me in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you are testifying here freely, without any problems? That's right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let me give you some explanation about the way we are going to proceed today. First, the Prosecutor will summarise what you said in your written statement. The Prosecutor will ask you to confirm a number of informations. He may show you a number of documents attached to your statement, and he may ask you other questions. The Prosecutor has half an hour to do all this. The two Judges sitting in front of you -- let me add that, normally speaking, there are three of us, but one of the Judges is not here today, so the two of us will then ask you questions, at least I am going to ask you a number of questions. As a general rule, when we have a witness here, the accused cross-examines the witness, but Mr. Seselj, for whatever reason, has decided not to cross-examine witnesses called under Rule 92 ter. This is a position adopted by Mr. Seselj and the Judges have nothing to say about this. That's the way we are going to proceed, madam. When you are asked a question, please try to answer very accurately, very specifically. If you do not understand the meaning of the question, do not hesitate to ask for the question to be rephrased. It's 10 past 12.00. We'll conclude today at a quarter past 1.00, so we'll start for about an hour. But if you feel unwell, Witness, do not hesitate to raise your hand and ask for the hearing to be stopped. But I hope that everything will run very smoothly. Mr. Prosecutor, it's for you now to start this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Good morning. I will begin with a short summary of the statement that the Prosecution seeks to admit under Rule 92 ter. At the beginning of the conflict, Jelena Radosevic was living with her family in Slatina, in western Slavonia. Because of the rising tensions between Croats and Serbs in Slatina, at the beginning of September 1991, the witness moved to Vocin. In Vocin, the witness worked as a nurse in the infirmary -- in an infirmary. At the beginning of October 1991, the witness saw seven buses in front of the former Sumarija company building in Vocin. On the front side of the buses were various flags. The witness also noticed armed men in front of the buses wearing olive-grey uniforms, with a fur hat on their head and a cockade. The witness later learned by talking to them that the soldiers who arrived with those buses were volunteers. A couple of days after their arrival, Radovan Novacic came to the infirmary. He presented himself as the commander of one of the volunteer units, and he told the witness that he had come to visit his wounded soldiers. The witness heard that his soldiers called him Vojvoda, and she concluded that he was the commander of Seselj's volunteers. Members of the Territorial Defence told Jelena Radosevic that the volunteers were mixed with members of their units; however, the volunteers were indisciplined, would not cooperate, and did not want to obey the orders of the TO Commander. They were rough, and the witness saw them drunk in the streets on a regular basis. On one occasion, sometime in November 1991, 14 volunteers came to the infirmary looking for Davor Jusufovic, a member of the Croatian Defence Forces, wounded in his shoulder. The volunteers were all very young, up to 25 years old, and had a white bird on their sleeve patches. One of the volunteers told the witness, "Hey, sister, we heard that one Ustasha is here. We would like to chop him to pieces." The witness did not allow them to see Davor, which made the volunteers very angry. They had a Serbian accent, were rough, and one of them even shot accidentally a bullet to the ground. At the end of November or in the first two days of December 1991, Vojislav Seselj came to Vocin. The witness noticed several cars parked in front of the building of the command, and a volunteer who was standing there told her that Seselj was in that building. She noticed that in front of the building there were military policemen dressed in blue uniforms. They wore white belts on which was written "Military Police." The witness heard from members of the Territorial Defence that on that occasion Seselj paid a visit to his soldiers in Lager Seculicia, Lisicine, and Ceralije. The witness believes that the main reason behind Mr. Seselj's visit was to give moral support to the volunteers. The witness is not aware of whether Seselj gave orders for civilians in Vocin to be killed. However, she did notice that the killing of Croat civilians started after his visit. Although very few Croats had been killed before Seselj's visit, the majority of Croat civilians were killed in two weeks after his visit in Vocin. Members of the Territorial Defence command were helpless and afraid of volunteers. The witness knew that JNA uniforms, weapons, and ammunitions were stored in the Catholic church in Vocin. She knew this because every time a Serb soldier got killed, as a nurse, she had to dress the victim with a JNA uniform before burial. She would get those uniforms from a man who told her that he collected them in the Catholic church. The witness was later told that the church was allegedly destroyed to prevent materiel and weapons from falling into the hands of Croatian forces. The witness left Vocin on 9 December 1991. When she left the volunteers were still in Vocin. Your Honours, this concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: So if you were asked questions about those events today, would you give the same answers that are contained in this statement?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly I would, yes. Except for some dates. I might have forgotten some dates. But otherwise, this is exactly how I experienced the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to move for the admission of the document bearing 65 ter number 5052 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 5052 shall be given Exhibit number P00580. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: I would also like to show to the witness a number of documents that are attached to her statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. There's a mistake on line 6. Mr. Registrar, could we have the number again. I believe it not transcribed correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 5052 shall be given the Exhibit number P00580. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Usher, could you now please display on the screen the document bearing the 65 ter number 834. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the document that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Could you please describe to the Trial Chamber what this document refers to.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a description of all those people who were victims on the 13th of December, 1991, in Vocin when we withdrew or during those days, 12th and 13th. Mostly people who were killed in Vocin on the 13th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Are you familiar with any of the people listed in the document?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly. I knew them all. I knew where they lived, and we all knew each other, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Are you aware of what the ethnic origin of the people listed in the document is?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps just two names on that list. Well, they are all Croats with the exception of two names perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would like to move for the admission of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter number 00834 shall be given Exhibit number P00581. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Usher, could you please now display on the screen the document bearing the 65 ter number 506 on the screen. For Your Honours' information, this is Exhibit number P431, which has already been admitted in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the document which is displayed on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a set of physician's findings and it relates to Kresimir Doric whom I knew. It is a medical report. And he was beaten up in Vocin. I know the doctor that signed this document. I also knew Kresimir Doric, and I know this, this is a document which is quite in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you. You just told us that you knew the victim. Are you aware of what the ethnic origin of the victim was?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Are you aware of what the ethnic origin of the perpetrator is?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean, the name mentioned here is a Serb name, of the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: I do not need to move for the admission of this document as it has already been admitted. Usher, could you please now display on the screen the document bearing the 65 ter number 498. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the document which is displayed on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Tribunal what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a document that shows that Antun Simic, whom I also knew, was beaten up in Vocin. I know him as well. I know the director who has signed here, and I know the people on the right-hand side, those who were the perpetrators in this incident. I knew all of them. And this is a truthful document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the ethnic origin of the victim is?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know what the ethnicity of the perpetrator is?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Usher, could you please display on the screen the document bearing the 65 ter number 07222C. Beg your pardon, Your Honours, I would like to tender into evidence the document that we just discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 498 shall be given Exhibit number P00582. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Could you please show the second page of this document. Usher, this is -- is this document number 07222C? Because I believe this is ... I have the ERN number of the document for your convenience. Or we can put the document in question on the ELMO. It would probably be easier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the picture which is displayed on the screen in front of you. Could you please describe to the Trial Chamber what this picture represents.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what is written here is "Main Staff, the Serbian Chetnik Movement." This is a skull and behind the skull are bones probably, bones of a corpse.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this patch before?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember now whether I did -- I'm not sure. I'm not sure. Now I'm no longer sure whether I had seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Do you remember if you have seen this patch, if at all, in Vocin, during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Vocin there were quite a few such emblems in 1991, quite a few. However, I cannot be sure now whether I recall this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Usher, could we now please display the document bearing the 65 ter number 07222D. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Witness, could you take a look at the picture which is displayed on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what this picture represents.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's written here "White Eagles Assault Battalion." It was one of the emblems that volunteers wore on their caps and on their shoulders, but I do remember it from Vocin in 1991. I did come across that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would like to move for the admission of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 07222D shall be given Exhibit number P00583. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, wasn't this document already in the exhibit -- in the list? Because a book has already been admitted in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Yes, the whole document has a 65 ter number, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And has been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: I don't believe it has been admitted into evidence. It has a 65 ter number but we submitted individual pages of this document. Usher, could you now please display the document bearing 65 ter number 07222E. Could you please display the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this picture?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. As for this patch, I also came across it in 1991. I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you. And where have you seen this patch?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did see it on the insignia of the Serb volunteers who came from Serbia. They wore that. Also, there were flags, but I remember this sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to move for the admission of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 07222E shall be given Exhibit number P00584. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: This is the last document I will show to the witness. Usher, could you now please display the document bearing the 65 ter number 4203 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Witness, could you please take a look at this picture. Do you remember having ever seen this picture, this flag, before?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right now, I cannot remember having seen it. I cannot state with certainty that it's somewhere in the recesses of my mind. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to put a number of questions to you. Where do you currently reside, in Croatia, in other country, in Serbia? Where do you live?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Croatia, in Slatina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You stated that you arrived in Vocin in 1991. Vocin is a small town. What was the population size in Vocin, roughly?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Slatina and I went to Vocin. That's 23 kilometres away from Slatina. Vocin is a village, and in 1991 it had a population of 1.700. In 1991, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you leave Slatina for Vocin? What is the reason for your departure?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for 20 or so years before that, I had lived in Slatina. And everything was all right up until 1990 or 1991 when this great fear was instilled in me. The HDZ won and I as a Serb felt very unsafe. We were threatened. My husband lost his job. At work it was quite difficult to deal with all the things that I had to deal with then, like the other Serbs in Slatina. That's why I went to Vocin, because I thought that's where my parents are, the population is Serb, and I thought that that would last only for a few days. So I thought that I should try to get away from something that I didn't even know what I would term it and what it would look like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just stated that the HDZ had won the elections and that you noticed a change in the atmosphere and that Serbs were under threat. That is why you decided to go to Vocin. To your knowledge, did Serbs in Slatina leave Slatina to go to Serbia or to another country?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It's not that we talked amongst ourselves, who was going where. We just knew that we were all afraid and that we wanted to go somewhere, somewhere where everybody individually would feel safe. I don't think it was only Serbia, because masses of people went to Hungary, to Bosnia. People went places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. At the time, did you hear that it was possible to exchange flats; for example, if you had a flat in Slatina as a Serb, you could exchange it with a Croat living in Serbia? Did you hear about that, about the possibility of exchanging property?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean then, in 1991? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you never heard about that at all?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You arrived in Vocin. In what month of 1991 did you arrive in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: I came to Vocin on the 4th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then you worked as nurse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not immediately, a few days afterwards. I wish to correct myself. The date was the 5th of September, if it matters. But I didn't go to work straightaway at this newly established centre. It was about 15 days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on you saw Serbs arrive. They carried weapons; they were wearing uniforms. In your view, why did they come to Vocin, these Serbs? What was their purpose? You haven't heard my question. Let me repeat it then.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't seem to hear something. I came to Vocin then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat my question. You were there and you saw Serbs arrive in Vocin. They were armed; they had uniforms. According to you, what was the purpose of these Serbs? Why did they come to Vocin?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since I worked in the medical profession and I was a civilian there, I don't know much about military things, but we, the population in Vocin, heard that they had come to help us in the conflict between the Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So they wanted to help the Serbs who lived in Vocin, I suppose. At some point in time you met with Radovan Novacic, a man aged about 35, and his men would call him Vojvoda. So if I understand correctly, you had a talk with him, you had a chat with him?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what did he tell you? What did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, he kept quiet. His head was down, and he kept quiet. When he walked into the room where we were working, he introduced himself and he said why he had come. Mostly he would sit there and keep quiet. He didn't talk, but we knew who he was and the soldiers who were there addressed him as Vojvoda, and he didn't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why are you saying that Radovan Novacic was, according to you, the commander of Seselj's volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: He introduced himself as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he actually stated, "I am the commander of Seselj's volunteers," that's how he introduced himself?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that he introduced himself that way when he introduced himself in terms of what his name was. He stayed at the infirmary for awhile and then he asked about his soldiers, who were there. And in this conversation, it's not that I asked him, but it was a very small room and all of us were doing something there and somebody asked him in what capacity he was there. Perhaps it was the wounded who had addressed him; I cannot recall that detail now. But I do know that what was said was that he was one of the commanders out there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So he was one of the commanders, but was it stated that he was the commander of Seselj's volunteers? It was something that somebody told you, but you didn't hear -- rather than Radovan Novacic tell it to you personally, didn't tell that to you personally?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: He said it and I heard it. The only difference was that I was not the one who had asked him. He said it and I heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. You heard it said. At the time did you know who Mr. Seselj was, or was it someone you didn't know at all?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no. I had heard of Mr. Seselj then, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when Radovan Novacic said that he was the commander of Seselj's volunteers, for you it was something rather normal? I mean, it didn't raise any questions in your mind, or did it?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: But of course it did. I immediately complained to him -- well, how should I put this? How do I describe this to you? I complained about this conduct of his soldiers that was not very nice, if I can put it that way. I remember that I was really happy to have the opportunity to meet someone to whom I could say that I was so afraid of these soldiers who were in the street and who behaved so improperly. And when they came to the infirmary, too, as the Prosecutor mentioned. Yes, yes, I did say that to him. Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what did he say?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing. He just shrugged his shoulders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in Vocin, there was the TO, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was the commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, who was the commander then? Now I'm not quite sure. Was it Rajko Bojcic or -- or I've already forgotten that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the ethnic composition of Vocin? Which ethnic group was in the majority? Was it the Croats or the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 there were 95 percent Serbs, and the remaining 5 percent were Croats. Perhaps it wasn't exactly 95 percent, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now know there was this commander of the TO. Did you see anyone from the JNA in Vocin, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see anyone from the JNA, but I know that people were talking at the time, November 1991, or somewhere around that time, that it was only Jovan Trbojevic who had come from the JNA. Now I've forgotten what rank he had, but he had a pretty high rank. He is the only one who had come in 1991 from Novi Sad, from the Novi Sad corps of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, you said that Jovan Trbojevic had a fight with the TO. Do you remember stating that or not?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps not exactly the way you just put it now, sir. It's not that they quarrelled, but there was discord. You could feel it, that there was this thing between the territorials and the JNA. There was something wrong there. I'm not the military type myself, but well, it's not that there was some kind of cooperation that could be seen or felt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a slight contradiction here. You said that there was no cooperation between the TO and the JNA, but at the same time you are saying that Colonel Trbojevic was on his own. Were there other men from the JNA there or not?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I do apologise to you. No one was there from the JNA except for Mr. Jovan Trbojevic. He had come from the JNA. The Territorial Defence is something different. I really wish to correct myself now. There was cooperation between the JNA and the territorials, but it's not that there was that much cooperation. I really do apologise to you. With the Serb volunteers, as far as I could feel, there wasn't that much of that there. What I'm saying now is quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have Serb volunteers who behave very badly, and if I remember properly, you stated in your statement that some of them were in prison and suddenly became volunteers. Did they mention that to you as well, because you took care of them? Did they tell you that they were in prison before becoming volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's the truth of it. There was a man called Ivan who was there in a bed. I didn't know his surname. He was 18 years old at the time. He came and said he was Ivan from Pancevo and that he was a Serb volunteer, and he came to us to the infirmary because he had jaundice. And I asked him, I asked him how come he was there when he was the same age as my daughter. I said, Have you done your military service? He said no. He said, No, sister, what military service, because for one month in prison, I get four months at liberty. And that's why I became very afraid when I heard from him that he had actually come to us from a prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now turn to the arrival of Mr. Seselj in Vocin. Did you see him arrive with your own eyes in Vocin, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who told you that he was there?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, stories were going around. People were talking about it on the streets, at work, in the bakery, everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, everyone was talking about it. Did he deliver a speech, or did he come and meet have with the volunteers and the local population? Do you remember that or not?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for the civilian local population, I don't know if he had a meeting with them, but people said that he had toured Sekolinci [phoen] which is where, as far as I was informed, was where his soldiers were put up, and he toured the rest of the terrain in Vocin where the soldiers were stationed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He went to see the soldiers, all right. You stated that in front of the building where he was, there were military policemen wearing belts. I was wondering whether these were JNA military policemen or TO military policemen. If there was no JNA in Vocin, who were these military policemen in your view?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were members of the TO, the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. They were members ever the TO. Fine. Why did you leave Vocin? For what reason did you leave Vocin in December? Why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: We left, or rather I left on the 9th of December 1991 -- 2, and I went with my husband to Belgrade to visit my children there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My fellow Judge has a few questions to put to you. I'm looking at the clock so I'm going to ask you one last question. You wrote three books. Two of them were confiscated by the Croats and we learned that you were imprisoned by the Croats. Why? For what reason were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was imprisoned in 1995, part of October and November, and I was imprisoned because, well, I don't know what article that was that I was sentenced by, but I was a rebel under some article and -- well, I've forgotten. I had to prove something but I forget what is it was now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What did you write in these books? Did you write these books to talk about your experience as a nurse, or did you write them to talk about your experience, because, I'm sorry, I haven't had the pleasure to read you. But why did you write these books? What was your purpose?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, because I was very sad at the time and I found it very difficult at the time, and I thought that only if I wrote it all down would I be able to remain normal and sane. That was a sort of defence mechanism that I used to defend myself from everything around me that was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Radosevic. I just have a couple of questions for you in relation to the link between -- please go ahead, if you need. The link between the beating up of your two friends that you named Kresimir Doric and Antun Simic. This happened, if I understand correctly, and I just want you to confirm, this happened well before the volunteers arrived to Vocin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So did you form any relation yourself between the beating up of these friends of yours and the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the beating up. In principle. Could not have had anything to do with the volunteers, could it? I just want to be sure that I've understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The other question I had to you was in relation to your mentioning of the Catholic church and I was just curious to know, why would, as I understand it, Serbs hide weapons, ammunition and uniforms in a Catholic church? Was it empty, or can you tell us a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, that's a good question. That's what I was wondering myself, many times. The church served as an institution -- as a religious institution, as a church in 1991. It was a Catholic church, a functioning Catholic church. Was it empty? Well, it was the same as any other church would look like for the services it held. And in 1991, I think I said that in my statement, I happened to learn due to force of circumstance that the TO had made a warehouse, a depot there. I didn't see it myself. But when we went to collect uniforms, then a person who was in charge of distributing -- I seem to be talking too fast again, all right. I apologise. When we went to collect our uniforms, as I was saying, then the person in charge of distributing the uniforms did bring those uniforms precisely from the church. And the church was mined in 1991. Probably the way I described it in my written statement, that's what the rumours going around were, so that the uniforms and weapons and whatever else that was there, I don't know, would come into the hands of the Croatian army. But I wondered why myself, because as far as I'm concerned, the church is always a religious edifice, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It does seem to be odd, doesn't it? But did you ever hear that also the Croatians and the Croatian army availed itself of the weapons and ammunition and uniforms that were available in the old TO depot in that church? Or was it only something that the Serbs used?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh dear, I don't think I can answer that question. Whether the Croats used it, too -- well, could you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question was, if you knew or heard of the ammunition and weapons and uniforms that were deposited in the old TO depot in the Catholic church, whether these things that were there were also used by the Croat army and the Croat Defence. You have told us that it was used by the Serbs, and I'm just curious to know whether also the Croats came there to pick up weapons or ammunition or uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, I understand you now. It was only the Serbs that used it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JELENA RADOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, thank you very much on behalf of the Trial Chamber for coming to testify here in The Hague. I wish you a very pleasant trip home. Before we adjourn, let me tell everyone that next week we'll be sitting in the afternoon, but on Thursday, the afternoon sitting will be transferred to the morning. In other words, on Thursday we'll be sitting in the morning. Please take good note of this. Mr. Seselj, please take note of the fact that we'll be sitting on Thursday in the morning and the two other days, in the afternoon. I wish you a very pleasant day.
